:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Normal modes of two coupled oscillators ($m = k = 1$, $\kappa = 0.2$). Left: level curves of the potential in the
plane of the displacements, the mode directions $(1, 1)$ (green) and $(1, -1)$ (red), and the trajectory starting at
$(1, 0)$ at rest (blue). Right: the same motion in time, a beat in which the oscillation passes from one mass to the
other. Generated by `figures/coupled_oscillators.sage`; the interactive version animates each mode and the
beat.](figures/coupled_oscillators.svg){#fig-coupled-oscillators width=95%}

{{< interactive coupled_oscillators 460 >}}

The free pair of masses is the simplest system with a zero mode. The first exercise finds both of its modes.

::: {#exr-clm-nm-free-pair}
#### Two masses and one spring

Find the normal modes of two masses $m$ on a line joined by a spring $\kappa$, and the general solution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M^{-1}K = \frac\kappa m\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $0$, eigenvector $(1, 1)$, and
$2\kappa/m$, eigenvector $(1, -1)$. For $\omega = 0$ the mode equation $\ddot Q = 0$ gives $Q = a + bt$ rather than a
cosine, so the general solution is $\eta = (a + bt)(1, 1) + c\cos(\sqrt{2\kappa/m}\,t + \delta)(1, -1)$: the centre of mass
moves uniformly while the separation oscillates.
:::

The coupled equations can also be solved directly, without first finding the modes. The second exercise does so with
`desolve_system` and recovers the beat of the figure.

::: {#exr-clm-nm-desolve}
#### Solving the coupled system

Solve $m\ddot x_1 = -(k + \kappa)x_1 + \kappa x_2$, $m\ddot x_2 = \kappa x_1 - (k + \kappa)x_2$ with $m = k = 1$, $\kappa =
1/5$, $x(0) = (1, 0)$, $\dot x(0) = 0$ using `desolve_system`, and compare with the beat $x_1 = \tfrac12(\cos\omega_1t +
\cos\omega_2t)$, $x_2 = \tfrac12(\cos\omega_1t - \cos\omega_2t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Laplace-transform solution of `desolve_system` agrees with the beat, with $\omega_1 = 1$ and $\omega_2 =
\sqrt{7/5}$:

{{< sage exr-clm-nm-desolve >}}
:::

A chain of masses has as many modes as masses, with frequencies that fill a band. The third exercise computes the
modes of three masses between two walls.

::: {#exr-clm-nm-chain}
#### A chain of three masses

Three masses $m$ in a row are joined to each other and to two walls by four springs $k$. With Sage, find the squared
frequencies and the modes, and compare with $\omega_j^2 = \frac{4k}{m}\sin^2\frac{j\pi}{8}$, $j = 1, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M^{-1}K = \frac km\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $\frac km(2 -
\sqrt2)$, $\frac{2k}{m}$, $\frac km(2 + \sqrt2)$ with modes $(1, \sqrt2, 1)$, $(1, 0, -1)$, $(1, -\sqrt2, 1)$, which are the
values $\frac{4k}{m}\sin^2\frac{j\pi}{8}$ and the sampled sines $\sin\frac{jn\pi}{4}$, $n = 1, 2, 3$:

{{< sage exr-clm-nm-chain >}}
:::

The closed forms of @exm-clb-chain-modes are easy to test against a numerical diagonalisation. The next exercise does it
with Sage for six masses.

::: {#exr-clb-chain-boundaries}
#### Checking the four boundary conditions

With Sage, build the stiffness matrices of a chain of $N = 6$ masses ($m = k = 1$) with fixed-fixed, free-free, periodic and fixed-free ends, compute the normal-mode
frequencies, and compare with the closed forms of @exm-clb-chain-modes [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problems 4.1-4.3].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A free end has one spring less, so its diagonal entry is $1$ instead of $2$; the periodic chain couples the last mass to the first:

{{< sage exr-clb-chain-boundaries >}}

The periodic chain has the degenerate pairs $\theta$, $2\pi - \theta$ (waves travelling both ways), and every boundary condition gives exactly $N$ frequencies in $[0, 2]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Changing one mass of a long chain changes its spectrum. The next exercise shows with Sage that a light impurity creates a
mode above the band, confined to a few masses.

::: {#exr-clb-mass-defect}
#### A light impurity

In a chain of $N = 101$ masses with fixed ends ($m = k = 1$) replace the middle mass by $\lambda m$. With Sage, find the highest mode for $\lambda = 1, 0.8, 0.5, 0.25, 2$
and measure how many masses take part in it. For $\lambda < 1$, show by the ansatz $u_n = (-1)^nr^{|n|}$ that an infinite chain has a mode of frequency
$2/\sqrt{\lambda(2 - \lambda)}$ with $r = \lambda/(2 - \lambda)$ [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.7].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Away from the defect the ansatz gives $\omega^2 = (1 + r)^2/r$; at the defect $\lambda\omega^2 = 2(1 + r)$. Dividing, $\lambda = 2r/(1 + r)$, so $r = \lambda/(2 - \lambda) < 1$ and $\omega^2 =
4/(\lambda(2 - \lambda)) > 4$. Numerically:

{{< sage exr-clb-mass-defect >}}

For $\lambda < 1$ the top mode leaves the band, its amplitudes decay geometrically with ratio $r$, and the participation ratio drops to a few masses: the mode is
localised. A heavy impurity ($\lambda = 2$) creates no mode above the band and the top mode stays extended.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The two-dimensional lattice is the Kronecker sum of two chains. The next exercise confirms the formula of
@exm-clb-square-lattice with Sage and counts the degenerate levels.

::: {#exr-clb-square-lattice}
#### The square lattice by machine

With Sage, build the $16 \times 16$ stiffness matrix of a $4 \times 4$ lattice with fixed edges ($m = k = 1$), compare its eigenvalues with $\omega_{pq}^2$ of @exm-clb-square-lattice,
and list the degenerate levels. Which degeneracy is not explained by $p \leftrightarrow q$? [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.12]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Using the Kronecker product for $C \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes C$:

{{< sage exr-clb-square-lattice >}}

The level $\omega^2 = 4$ has multiplicity four: besides $(p, q) = (1, 4), (4, 1)$ it contains $(2, 3), (3, 2)$, since $\sin^2\frac{\pi}{10} + \sin^2\frac{4\pi}{10} = \sin^2\frac{2\pi}{10} +
\sin^2\frac{3\pi}{10} = 1$: whenever $p + q = N + 1$ the two angles $\tfrac{p\pi}{2(N + 1)}$, $\tfrac{q\pi}{2(N + 1)}$ are complementary, an accidental degeneracy.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

For the two coupled oscillators everything can be computed in closed form. The proposition records the frequencies,
the beat and the separate conservation of the mode energies, together with the triatomic molecule.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-clm-normal-modes}
#### Normal modes of coupled oscillators

For two masses $m$ with springs $k, \kappa, k$ (@exm-clm-nm-two-masses) the normal modes are $(1, 1)$ with $\omega_1^2 =
k/m$ and $(1, -1)$ with $\omega_2^2 = (k + 2\kappa)/m$; the solution with $x(0) = (1, 0)$, $\dot x(0) = 0$ is the beat
$x_1 = \tfrac12(\cos\omega_1t + \cos\omega_2t)$, $x_2 = \tfrac12(\cos\omega_1t - \cos\omega_2t)$; in the normal coordinates
$Q_{1, 2} = (x_1 \pm x_2)/\sqrt2$ the energy splits into two separately conserved mode energies. For the linear
triatomic molecule with masses $m, M, m$ and springs $k$ the squared frequencies are $0$, $k/m$ and $k(1/m + 2/M)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/coupled_oscillators.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When the coupling is weak the two frequencies are close and the beat is slow. The energy then passes back and forth
between the masses over many oscillations.

::: {#exm-clm-nmp-weak-coupling}
#### Weak coupling

For $\kappa \ll k$, $\omega_2 = \omega_1\sqrt{1 + 2\kappa/k} \approx \omega_1(1 + \kappa/k)$, so the energy passes from one
mass to the other and back in the beat period $2\pi/(\omega_2 - \omega_1) \approx 2\pi k/(\omega_1\kappa)$. For $m = k =
1$, $\kappa = 0.2$ this is $2\pi/(\sqrt{1.4} - 1) \approx 34$ (estimate $10\pi \approx 31$), the envelope period in
@fig-coupled-oscillators.
:::

In normal coordinates the two oscillators decouple completely. Each normal coordinate is then an independent harmonic
oscillator with its own conserved energy.

::: {#exm-clm-nmp-normal-coordinates}
#### Normal coordinates

With $Q_{1, 2} = (x_1 \pm x_2)/\sqrt2$, $L_2 = \tfrac m2(\dot Q_1^2 - \omega_1^2Q_1^2) + \tfrac m2(\dot Q_2^2 - \omega_2^2Q_2^2)$,
because $x_1^2 + x_2^2 = Q_1^2 + Q_2^2$ and $(x_1 - x_2)^2 = 2Q_2^2$: two independent oscillators, each with its own
conserved energy (@prp-clm-normal-modes).
:::

The triatomic molecule's modes can be checked by substituting the vectors. The centre of mass stays at rest in both
stretching modes, as it must for vibrations of an isolated molecule.

::: {#exm-clm-nmp-molecule-modes}
#### Shapes of the molecular modes

With $K = k\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and the mass matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(m, M, m)$, the vector $(1, 0, -1)$ has $K$-image $k(1, 0, -1)$ and mass-image $m(1, 0, -1)$, so
$\omega^2 = k/m$; the vector $(1, -2m/M, 1)$ has $K$-image $k(1 + 2m/M)(1, -2, 1)$ and mass-image $m(1, -2, 1)$, so
$\omega^2 = k(1/m + 2/M)$ (@exr-clm-nmp-molecule-check). Both stretches have $m\eta_1 + M\eta_2 + m\eta_3 = 0$: the
centre of mass is at rest.
:::

Real oscillators are damped. The next example shows that equal damping on every mass keeps the normal modes, each
decaying at the same rate.

::: {#exm-clb-uniform-damping}
#### Uniform damping keeps the modes

Add the friction $-2\beta m\dot x_j$ to each of $N$ equal masses. The equations $M\ddot x + 2\beta M\dot x + Kx = 0$ are diagonalised by the same normal coordinates as
without damping, and each mode obeys $\ddot Q + 2\beta\dot Q + \omega_p^2Q = 0$: it oscillates at $\sqrt{\omega_p^2 - \beta^2}$ and decays as $e^{-\beta t}$. All masses of a mode
still move with a common frequency. If the damping coefficients differ from mass to mass, the damping matrix no longer commutes with $M^{-1}K$ and
damping mixes the modes [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.8].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The long-wavelength modes of a chain are sound waves. The next example takes the continuum limit and shows what the two
kinds of ends do to a travelling pulse.

::: {#exm-clb-chain-sound}
#### Sound in a chain and reflection at its ends

For $\theta \ll 1$, $\omega \approx \sqrt{k/m}\,\theta$: with spacing $a$ and wave number $\kappa = \theta/a$, $\omega = v\kappa$ with the speed of sound $v = a\sqrt{k/m}$, and a
long chain carries pulses without distortion, like the string of the wave equation. At a fixed end the displacement vanishes and a pulse is reflected
inverted; at a free end the force vanishes and it is reflected upright; on a periodic chain it goes round without reflection. Short wavelengths,
$\theta$ near $\pi$, are dispersed: their group velocity $v\cos(\theta/2)$ goes to zero at the band edge [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The beat can be rewritten as a fast oscillation inside a slow envelope. The first exercise performs this rewriting
with the sum-to-product formulas.

::: {#exr-clm-nmp-beat-envelope}
#### The envelope of the beat

With $\bar\omega = (\omega_1 + \omega_2)/2$ and $\Delta = \omega_2 - \omega_1$, show that the beat of @prp-clm-normal-modes is
$x_1 = \cos(\Delta t/2)\cos\bar\omega t$, $x_2 = \sin(\Delta t/2)\sin\bar\omega t$, and find when mass 1 is at rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos a + \cos b = 2\cos\frac{a + b}2\cos\frac{a - b}2$ and $\cos a - \cos b = -2\sin\frac{a + b}2\sin\frac{a - b}2$, with
$a = \omega_1t$, $b = \omega_2t$, $\frac{a - b}{2} = -\frac{\Delta t}{2}$. The amplitude of mass 1 is $|\cos(\Delta t/2)|$,
which vanishes at $t = \pi/\Delta$: then all the energy is in mass 2, whose amplitude $|\sin(\Delta t/2)|$ is $1$.
:::

The second exercise verifies the molecular modes by direct substitution. It is a check of the generalised eigenvalue
equation @eq-normal-modes.

::: {#exr-clm-nmp-molecule-check}
#### The molecular modes

Verify $Ka = \omega^2\operatorname{diag}(m, M, m)\,a$ for the three modes of @exm-clm-nmp-molecule-modes, including the translation $(1, 1, 1)$
with $\omega = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $D = \operatorname{diag}(m, M, m)$ for the mass matrix. $K(1, 1, 1) = 0$. $K(1, 0, -1) = k(1, 0, -1)$ and $D(1, 0, -
1) = m(1, 0, -1)$, so $\omega^2 = k/m$. For $a = (1, -2m/M, 1)$: $Ka = k(1 + 2m/M, -2 - 4m/M, 1 + 2m/M) = k(1 + 2m/M)(1,
-2, 1)$ and $Da = (m, -2m, m) = m(1, -2, 1)$, so $\omega^2 = \frac km(1 + 2m/M) = k(1/m + 2/M)$.
:::

The double pendulum linearised about its lowest position has two modes. The third exercise computes them with Sage
from the metric of @exr-clm-lagrangian-double-pendulum.

::: {#exr-clm-nmp-double-pendulum}
#### Small oscillations of the double pendulum

For $m_1 = m_2 = m$ and $l_1 = l_2 = l$, linearise the double pendulum about $\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 0$ and find its normal
modes with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M = ml^2\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $K = mgl\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, and $\det(K -
\omega^2M) = 0$ gives $\omega^2 = (2 \mp \sqrt2)g/l$, with modes $(1, \pm\sqrt2)$: in the slow mode the two rods swing
together, in the fast one in opposite directions:

{{< sage exr-clm-nmp-double-pendulum >}}
:::

A driven chain responds strongly at its normal frequencies and not at all at certain others. The next exercise finds
these anti-resonances for two masses.

::: {#exr-clb-antiresonance}
#### Anti-resonance

Two masses $m$ are joined to each other and to two walls by three springs $k$, and the first is driven by $F_0\cos\omega t$. Find the steady-state amplitude $X_1(\omega)$
of the driven mass, its resonances and the frequency where $X_1 = 0$. Interpret the zero [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.9].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x_j = X_j\cos\omega t$: $(2k - m\omega^2)X_1 - kX_2 = F_0$ and $-kX_1 + (2k - m\omega^2)X_2 = 0$, so
$$
X_1 = \frac{F_0(2k - m\omega^2)}{(2k - m\omega^2)^2 - k^2} .
$$
It diverges at the normal frequencies $\omega^2 = k/m$ and $3k/m$ (@prp-clm-normal-modes with $\kappa = k$) and vanishes at $\omega^2 = 2k/m$, the frequency of the second mass
alone with the first held fixed: the second mass then oscillates so that its spring exactly cancels the drive on the first. Between any two resonances
of the driven site there is one anti-resonance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The modes of a damped chain are simple when the damping is uniform. The next exercise asks exactly when damping keeps
the normal modes in general.

::: {#exr-clb-damped-modes}
#### When damping keeps the modes

For $M\ddot x + D\dot x + Kx = 0$ with symmetric positive $M$, $D$, $K$, show that the undamped normal modes diagonalise the equation iff $DM^{-1}K = KM^{-1}D$ (for example
$D = \alpha M + \beta K$). Give a two-mass example with damping on one mass only where the modes mix [@foulaadvand2023computational, Problem 4.8].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $y = M^{1/2}x$ the equation becomes $\ddot y + \tilde D\dot y + \tilde Ky = 0$ with $\tilde D = M^{-1/2}DM^{-1/2}$, $\tilde K = M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ symmetric. The eigenvectors of $\tilde K$ (the modes)
diagonalise $\tilde D$ iff $\tilde D$ and $\tilde K$ commute, which is $DM^{-1}K = KM^{-1}D$. Rayleigh damping $D = \alpha M + \beta K$ qualifies. For the two masses of
@prp-clm-normal-modes with $D = \operatorname{diag}(\gamma, 0)$, $\tilde D$ has the off-diagonal element $\gamma/2m$ in the mode basis $(1, \pm1)/\sqrt2$, which couples the in-phase and
out-of-phase modes: energy leaks from one mode into the other.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Oscillations on the sphere and on $SU(2)$

On a curved configuration space the kinetic matrix $M$ of @eq-linearised-lagrangian is the metric at the equilibrium.
The method is unchanged, but the chart must be regular at the equilibrium, and symmetries of the potential that fix
the equilibrium force frequencies to coincide.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-clm-curved-oscillations}
#### Small oscillations on the sphere and on $SU(2)$

At an equilibrium $q_0$ of $L = \tfrac12 mg_{ij}\dot q^i\dot q^j - V$, in any chart regular at $q_0$, the squared
frequencies are the eigenvalues of $(mg(q_0))^{-1}\operatorname{Hess}V(q_0)$. For the spherical pendulum (a mass $m$ on
the sphere of radius $l$ with $V = mgZ$) they are $g/l$, twice, at the lowest point. For a unit-mass particle on $SU(2)$,
with the metric of the unit three-sphere (@eq-su2-gram) and $V = k(1 - \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}U)$, they are $k$, three
times, at $U = \mathbb{1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/coupled_oscillators.sage`), in the charts $(X, Y)$ of the
sphere and $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$ of $U = a_0 + i\vec a\cdot\vec\sigma$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The spherical pendulum near its lowest point is a two-dimensional isotropic oscillator. Its two frequencies coincide
because the potential is symmetric under rotations about the vertical.

::: {#exm-clm-co-spherical-pendulum}
#### The spherical pendulum

In the chart $(X, Y)$ near the bottom, $Z = -\sqrt{l^2 - X^2 - Y^2}$, so $M = m\mathbb{1}$ and $K = \frac{mg}{l}\mathbb{1}$
at $X = Y = 0$: $\omega^2 = g/l$ twice. Small motions are ellipses about the bottom, the orbits of
@exm-clm-central-oscillator; the degeneracy comes from the rotations about the vertical, which fix the bottom
(@exr-clm-co-spherical-sage).
:::

On $SU(2)$ the potential depends only on the trace, which is invariant under conjugation. Conjugation fixes the
identity and rotates its tangent space, and this forces three equal frequencies.

::: {#exm-clm-co-su2}
#### A particle on $SU(2)$

$V = k(1 - \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}U) = k(1 - a_0)$ is invariant under $U \mapsto hUh^{-1}$, which fixes $\mathbb{1}$ and
acts on the tangent space $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ there as $SO(3)$ (@sec-lie-algebras). Near $\mathbb{1}$, $a_0 = \sqrt{1 - |
\vec a|^2} \approx 1 - \tfrac12|\vec a|^2$, so $L_2 = \tfrac12|\dot{\vec a}|^2 - \tfrac k2|\vec a|^2$: a three-dimensional
isotropic oscillator, a triplet of modes with $\omega^2 = k$.
:::

Without a potential every point is an equilibrium and every frequency vanishes. The motion near any point is then
the geodesic motion of @exm-el-sphere, which neither returns nor runs away exponentially.

::: {#exm-clm-co-free-sphere}
#### The free particle on the sphere

With $V = 0$ every point of $S^2$ is an equilibrium with $K = 0$, so all frequencies vanish: two zero modes, one for
each independent rotation moving the point. A small push sends the particle along a great circle at constant speed,
the neutral, linear-in-time drift of a zero mode (@exr-clm-nm-free-pair).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The frequencies do not depend on the chart, because at a critical point the Hessian transforms as a tensor. The first
exercise proves this.

::: {#exr-clm-co-chart-independence}
#### The Hessian at a critical point

For a change of chart $x = x(y)$, show that $\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial y^a\partial y^b} = \frac{\partial x^i}{\partial
y^a}\frac{\partial x^j}{\partial y^b}\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial x^i\partial x^j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial x^i}
\frac{\partial^2x^i}{\partial y^a\partial y^b}$, and deduce that the eigenvalues of $g^{-1}\operatorname{Hess}V$ at a
critical point are the same in both charts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The formula is the chain rule applied twice. At a critical point the last term vanishes, so $\operatorname{Hess}_yV =
J^{\mathsf T}(\operatorname{Hess}_xV)J$ with $J = \partial x/\partial y$; the metric transforms the same way, $g_y =
J^{\mathsf T}g_xJ$. Then $g_y^{-1}\operatorname{Hess}_yV = J^{-1}(g_x^{-1}\operatorname{Hess}_xV)J$, a similar matrix with
the same eigenvalues.
:::

Spherical coordinates are singular at the poles, so they cannot be used directly at the bottom of the sphere. The
second exercise works around this with polar-like coordinates in the tangent plane.

::: {#exr-clm-co-spherical-sage}
#### The spherical pendulum in angles

With $\alpha$ the angle from the downward vertical and $\varphi$ the azimuth, $L = \tfrac12 ml^2(\dot\alpha^2 + \sin^2\alpha\,
\dot\varphi^2) + mgl\cos\alpha$. Substitute $u = \alpha\cos\varphi$, $v = \alpha\sin\varphi$ and show with Sage that to
second order $L = \tfrac12 ml^2(\dot u^2 + \dot v^2) - \tfrac12 mgl(u^2 + v^2) + mgl$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot\alpha^2 + \alpha^2\dot\varphi^2 = \dot u^2 + \dot v^2$ and $\sin^2\alpha = \alpha^2 + O(\alpha^4)$, while $\cos\alpha = 1 -
\tfrac12(u^2 + v^2) + O(\alpha^4)$; the quadratic Lagrangian is the isotropic oscillator with $\omega^2 = g/l$:

{{< sage exr-clm-co-spherical-sage >}}
:::

The trace of $U$ is simple in the Euler angles of @eq-euler-angles. The third exercise computes it with Sage and
explains why the Euler chart cannot be used for the small oscillations of @exm-clm-co-su2.

::: {#exr-clm-co-su2-euler}
#### The potential in Euler angles

With $T_a = -\tfrac i2\sigma_a$ and $U = e^{\varphi T_3}e^{\theta T_1}e^{\psi T_3}$, show with Sage that $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}U =
\cos\frac\theta2\cos\frac{\varphi + \psi}2$. Where is $V = k(1 - \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}U)$ minimal, and why is the
Euler chart unsuitable there?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The minimum $V = 0$ is at $\theta = 0$, $\varphi + \psi = 0$ (mod $4\pi$), that is $U = \mathbb{1}$. There the chart
degenerates (@exm-su2-chart): only $\varphi + \psi$ is defined and $\det G = \sin^2\theta/64$ vanishes, so $M$ is singular
and the method needs a regular chart such as $(a_1, a_2, a_3)$:

{{< sage exr-clm-co-su2-euler >}}
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-classical-mechanics-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises below combine the sections of this chapter. Each follows one system through several formalisms:
the Kepler problem, the spherical pendulum and the free particle on $SU(2)$.

::: {#exr-clm-int-kepler}
#### The Kepler problem in every formalism

For a particle in the plane with $V = -k/r$: (a) write the Lagrangian in polar coordinates and identify the Noether
charges of rotations and time translations; (b) write the Hamiltonian and check that $L$ and $\vec A$ have vanishing
brackets with it; (c) integrate Hamilton's equations numerically with Sage from $(x, y, p_x, p_y) = (1, 0, 0, 0.8)$
($m = k = 1$) and check that $E$, $L$ and $\vec A$ stay constant and that the orbit is the conic with $e = |\vec A|$;
(d) explain with @exr-clm-circular-orbit why the orbit closes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $L = \tfrac12 m(\dot r^2 + r^2\dot\varphi^2) + k/r$; $\varphi$ is cyclic, so $p_\varphi = mr^2\dot\varphi$ is conserved
(rotations), and time translation gives $E = \tfrac12 m(\dot r^2 + r^2\dot\varphi^2) - k/r$ (@exm-charge-energy). (b) $H
= \frac{p_r^2}{2m} + \frac{p_\varphi^2}{2mr^2} - \frac kr$, and $\{L_z, H\} = 0$, $\{A_i, H\} = 0$ (@exr-clm-poisson-lrl).
(c) The start is the aphelion: $E = 0.32 - 1 = -0.68$, $L = 0.8$, $p = L^2 = 0.64$, $\vec A = (p_yL - 1, 0) = (-0.36, 0)$,
$e = 0.36$, and $a = p/(1 - e^2) = 1/(2|E|) \approx 0.735$; the numerical orbit keeps $E$, $L$ and $\vec A$ constant and
satisfies $r(1 + e\cos(\varphi - \pi)) = p$:

{{< sage exr-clm-int-kepler >}}

(d) Radial and angular frequencies coincide for $1/r$ (@exr-clm-circular-orbit), so $r$ returns to its value after
exactly one revolution; equivalently, the conserved $\vec A$ fixes the direction of the pericentre.
:::

The second exercise treats the spherical pendulum, which combines a curved configuration space, a cyclic coordinate
and an effective potential. It needs no computer algebra.

::: {#exr-clm-int-spherical-pendulum}
#### The spherical pendulum

A mass $m$ moves on a sphere of radius $l$ in uniform gravity; use the angle $\alpha$ from the downward vertical and the
azimuth $\varphi$. (a) Write $L$ and $H$. (b) Find two conserved quantities with Noether's theorem and check their
Poisson brackets with $H$. (c) Reduce to one-dimensional motion in an effective potential $U(\alpha)$. (d) Find the
conical motions $\alpha = \alpha_0$ and the frequency of small oscillations about them, and compare with
@exm-clm-co-spherical-pendulum as $\alpha_0 \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $L = \tfrac12 ml^2(\dot\alpha^2 + \sin^2\alpha\,\dot\varphi^2) + mgl\cos\alpha$ and $H = \frac{p_\alpha^2}{2ml^2} +
\frac{p_\varphi^2}{2ml^2\sin^2\alpha} - mgl\cos\alpha$. (b) $\varphi$ is cyclic: $p_\varphi = ml^2\sin^2\alpha\,\dot\varphi$
(rotations about the vertical) and $H$ (time translation) are conserved; $\{p_\varphi, H\} = -\partial H/\partial\varphi = 0$.
(c) $E = \frac{p_\alpha^2}{2ml^2} + U(\alpha)$ with $U = \frac{p_\varphi^2}{2ml^2\sin^2\alpha} - mgl\cos\alpha$. (d) $U'(\alpha_0)
= 0$ gives $p_\varphi^2 = m^2gl^3\sin^4\alpha_0/\cos\alpha_0$, so $\dot\varphi^2 = g/(l\cos\alpha_0)$, the conical pendulum.
Then $U''(\alpha_0) = \frac{p_\varphi^2}{ml^2}\cdot\frac{3\cos^2\alpha_0 + \sin^2\alpha_0}{\sin^4\alpha_0} + mgl\cos\alpha_0$, which
with the value of $p_\varphi^2$ is $\frac{mgl}{\cos\alpha_0}(1 + 3\cos^2\alpha_0)$, so $\omega_\alpha^2 = U''/(ml^2) = \frac gl\cdot
\frac{1 + 3\cos^2\alpha_0}{\cos\alpha_0}$. As $\alpha_0 \to 0$, $\omega_\alpha^2 \to 4g/l$ and $\dot\varphi^2 \to g/l$: the radial
frequency is twice the angular one, as for the isotropic oscillator of @exr-clm-circular-orbit, which the pendulum
becomes near the bottom (@exm-clm-co-spherical-pendulum).
:::

The third exercise treats the free particle on the group $SU(2)$. Its Lagrangian comes from the metric of the
three-sphere in Euler angles, and its motions are the one-parameter subgroups and their translates.

::: {#exr-clm-int-su2}
#### The free particle on $SU(2)$

Take $L = \tfrac12 G_{ij}\dot q^i\dot q^j$ with the Gram matrix $G$ of @eq-su2-gram in the Euler angles $(\theta, \varphi,
\psi)$. (a) Find two cyclic coordinates and their conserved momenta. (b) Compute $H = \tfrac12 G^{ij}p_ip_j$ with Sage.
(c) Show with Sage that $(\theta, \varphi, \psi) = (\theta_0, \varphi_0 + t, \psi_0)$, the curve $e^{tT_3}U_0$, solves
Hamilton's equations for every $\theta_0 \in (0, \pi)$. (d) What are the small oscillations of a free particle on $SU(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $G$ depends on $\theta$ only, so $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are cyclic: $p_\varphi = \tfrac14(\dot\varphi + \cos\theta\,\dot\psi)$
and $p_\psi = \tfrac14(\dot\psi + \cos\theta\,\dot\varphi)$ are conserved, the charges of left and right multiplication by
$e^{sT_3}$. (b) $H = 2\left(p_\theta^2 + \frac{p_\varphi^2 - 2\cos\theta\,p_\varphi p_\psi + p_\psi^2}{\sin^2\theta}\right)$.
(c) The momenta of the curve are $(0, \tfrac14, \tfrac14\cos\theta_0)$, constant, and $\partial H/\partial\theta = 0$ there, so
$\dot p_\theta = 0$, while $\dot q = G^{-1}p = (0, 1, 0)$: a geodesic, the left translate of a one-parameter subgroup by
$U_0$:

{{< sage exr-clm-int-su2 >}}

(d) With $V = 0$ every point is an equilibrium and all three frequencies vanish (@exm-clm-co-free-sphere); a potential
such as $k(1 - \tfrac12\operatorname{tr}U)$ lifts them to $\omega^2 = k$ (@prp-clm-curved-oscillations).
:::
::::
